The house resumed from April 30 consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, to amend the Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinfret-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Application to court and issue of certificate.

Last evening I was discussing this measure and I had briefly referred to the circumstances that led up to the passing of the legislation in 1914. Possibly I should have pointed out that in 1914 we enacted a statute which was drafted by the draftsman of the British parliament. During the progress of the discussion at that time the matter was considered in detail and certain observations' were made as to the drafting of the measure, whereupon Mr. Borden, now Sir Robert Borden, directed the attention of the house to the fact to which I have just alluded, namely, that the measure had been drafted in Great Britain. The reason was obvious. This is a very serious obligation imposed upon the British Empire, and as the taxpayer in Great Britain is so much concerned, inasmuch as he largely makes possible the maintenance of the fleet that insures the safety of our citizens on the high seas, the drafting of the bill became a matter of paramount importance. When the measure was introduced in the legislature of each of the various self-governing communities composing the empire it was the same in terms, except for such variations only as might be essential in view of the conditions under which these respective communities live.
The Naturalization Act divides itself into two branches: first there is the question of principle under which naturalization may be granted; and secondly the act relates to procedure. Those who are interested in the matter will find in our revised statutes the act set out as it now exists. In 1919 we made some amendments to the statute. It is unnecessary to do more than point out that we have set up conditions under which naturalization may be granted. These conditions I will refer to for the reason that it becomes important to consider them
2544	COMMONS
Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
in the light of what was done by the other communities of the empire, and in view also of the observations made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret), which I regret to say he must have made inadvertently, because a mere casual observation of the legislation of other portions of the empire will show that the hon. gentleman is wholly wrong.
The statute in question is now chapter 138 of the Act respecting British Nationality, Naturalization and Aliens. The section relating to the question of principle is' section 4:
The minister may grant a certificate of naturalization to an alien who makes an application for the purpose, and satisfies the minister-
(a)	That he has either resided in His Majesty's dominions for a period of not less than five years in the manner required by this section, or been in the service of the crown for not less than five years, within the last eight years before the application; and
(b)	that he is of good character and has an adequate knowledge of either the English or French languages; and
(c)	that he intends if his application is granted either to reside in His Majesty's dominions or to enter or continue in the service of the crown.
Then follows the provision respecting residence required. It is residence in Canada for not less than one year immediately preceding the application, and previous residence, either in Canada or in some other part of His Majesty's dominions, for a period of four years within the last eight years before the application.
The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the minister, and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
(4)	A certificate of naturalization shall not take effect until the applicant has taken the oath of allegiance.
(5)	In the case of a woman who was a British subject previously to her marriage to an alien and whose husband has died, or whose marriage has been dissolved, the requirements of this section as to residence shall not apply, and the minister may, in any other special ease, if he thinks fit, grant a certificate of naturalization, although the four years' residence or five years' service has not been within the last eight years before the application.
(6)	For the purposes of this section a period spent in the service of the crown may, if the minister thinks fit, be treated as equivalent to a period of residence in Canada.
This embodies the amendments of 1914, enacted after t'he outbreak of the war, and also those of 1920, which I think many hon members will recall. It is the principle upon which naturalization is granted to an alien in this country, conferring upon him the status

of a British subject throughout the world, with all the immunities, the rights and the powers that belong to such a subject. Now comes the next question-the conditions under which this privilege may be granted. There is a provision dealing with procedure -and evidence, commencing at section 22 and including the following sections down to section 28. The section, I have read having settled the principle, we now apply procedure and evidence and these matters are dealt with as follows:
22.	An alien desiring to be naturalized shall apply for a decision establishing that he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this act to any judge of any superior court or to any judge of any circuit, district or county court, and in the province of Ontario the court of general sessions of the peace, and in the Northwest Territories to such authorities or persons as the governor in council may prescribe.
23.	The application shall be delivered at the office of the clerk or other proper officer of the court during office hours, and such application shall be posted by such clerk or other proper officer in a conspicuous place in his office, continuously for a period of at least three months before the application is heard by the court.
That is the second provision, with respect to procedure. To continue:
24.	At any time after the filing of such application and previous to the hearing of the application, any person objecting to the naturalization of the alien may file in court an opposition in which shall be stated the grounds of his objection.
25.	The applicant shall produce to the court such evidence, that- he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this act, as the court may require, and shall also personally appear before the court for examination unless it is established to the satisfaction of the court that he is prevented from so appearing by some good and sufficient cause.
26.	If the court decides that the alien is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and possesses the required qualifications, a certified copy of such decision shall be transmitted by the clerk of the court to the minister together with the application and such other papers, documents and reports as may be required by any regulation made hereunder.
27.	The minister may thereupon in his absolute discretion issue a certificate of naturalization and shall send the same to the clerk of the court to whom the application for naturalization was made.
(2) Upon the applicant taking and subscribing the oath of allegiance, which may be so taken and subscribed by any person duly authorized to administer judicial oaths by the laws of the province in which the applicant resides, the clerk shall deliver the certificate to the applicant.
Those are the conditions as to procedure under which the principles to which I have referred are made applicable. It was suggested that this appearing in court was a

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
difficult matter. I dealt with that in 1914, and if any hon. gentlemen are curious and desire to see what is the law in the United States, if they are not bored by reading my observations at that time they will find that applicants must appear in open court, supported by two witnesses in open court, who must give evidence as to their character and their fitness to become American citizens, and the applicant must publicly renounce his allegiance to his former sovereign and former country. Further than that, in open court he must take an oath that he does believe in organized government and that he is not a member of any organization or society which has in mind the destruction of governments. Those are parts of the conditions which are imposed in the United States.
We have imposed less onerous conditions in Canada, under the sections which I have just read and which it is now proposed to repeal. There is not another word substituted; there is not another suggestion made to take the place of these sections. We are just leaving it in the hands of the Secretary of State with the power to make regulations, and I say to him if he had taken the trouble to read the laws of the other parts of the British Empire he would not have said what he did last evening. Canada is not the only country which has made these provisions with respect to procedure, and first we will consider the nearby country of Newfoundland. They passed the same statute; they had to deal with the same matter, and what action did they take? In 1915, having enacted the substantial provisions with respect to principle to which I have just alluded, we find them further providing for these cases. The first sections only deal with the manner in which they may be dealt with, and I will not read them again. Section 19 of chapter 11 of the statutes of 1915 of Newfoundland reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations generally for carrying into effect the objects of this act, and in particular with respect to the following matters:
(a)	The form and registration of certificates of naturalization granted by the Colonial Secretary;
(b)	The form and registration of declarations of alienage and declarations of resumption or retention of British nationality;
(e) The time within which the oath of allegiance is to be taken. . . .
And so on. Then there is a provision with respect to proof of certificates and with respect to the evidence of declarations. In other words, the colony of Newfoundland dealt with the matter of procedure through
the regulations which might be made by the colonial secretary or the governor in council.
Will my hon. friend allow me to interrupt? That will be exactly the situation in Canada if this bill passes.

Yes, in part; I am coming to that. Now let us consider New Zealand. That country passed a statute in 1923, after the war, to amend and consolidate the former legislation, and that statute embodies certain provisions now found in our revised statutes. They have the same provisions with respect to the principle which we now have in Canada, and then comes section 4 of their act:
When any alien friend

That is different from our statute.
-residing in New Zealand desires to be naturalized as a British subject in New Zealand, he may present to the minister an application in writing signed by him, setting forth-	.
(a)	His name, age, birthplace, residence,
occupation, and nationality:	_
(b)	The length of his residence in New Zealand and his desire to settle therein either permanently or for a limited period, stating such limited period (if any):
(e) A request that a certificate of naturalization may be granted to him.
(2) Every such application shall be verified by a statutory declaration subscribed by the applicant.
Then section 5 continues:
(1)	If the minister is satisfied-
(a)	That the applicant has either resided within New Zealand for a period not less than the prescribed time or has been in the service of the crown in any part of His Majesty's dominions for not less than five years within the last eight years; and
(b)	That the applicant is of good character and has an adequate knowledge of the English language; and
(c)	That the applicant intends, if his application is granted, to continue to reside in His Majesty's dominions, or to enter, or continue in, the service of the crown; and
(d)	That in all other respects the applicant is a person fit to hold and exercise the rights of a British subject in New Zealand-the minister may grant a certificate of naturalization to the applicant.
(2) The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the minister, and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.

If my hon. friend will
allow me, all these dispositions will remain in the law when we have repealed the sections referring the cases to the courts.

I am coming to just
what my hon. friend is leaving out; I am

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
pointing out that we are leaving to regulation what is now a matter of statute in part in the other British communities. Further, we are doing what is not being done in any other part of this empire. It is true that there is a broad power in our section 28 which I mentioned with respect to regulations ; that section was drafted in Great Britain and sent to Canada and all the other self-governing communities throughout the world where our empire extends. That is the position, and with the reason for the absolute discretion resting with the minister I shall presently deal, but it is not a political discretion. To that I shall also refer.
It is not so intended.

It should not be, but it
will be; we have had some experience in these things.

I do not think any
Secretary of State from either side of the house would so act.

I did not mention the
Secretary of State. While I am on the subject of New Zealand and Australia, I would mention that a representative of New Zealand was here the other day, and he explained to us that the population of New Zealand is between 95 per cent and 100 per cent British, and that in Australia the population is over 90 per cent of British origin. That is the reason why I dealt with those two countries first, because they are exactly similar to Great Britain; they have a solid British population with only one language to consider, and the conditions under which naturalization certificates are to be granted are vastly different from those which obtain in this country, to which we have invited hundreds of thousands of people of practically every race in the world.
Now let me go to the Union of South Africa. I was very curious about that country, because there they have two languages also. I have in my hand a copy of the statutes of South Africa, which are printed in English on one page and in Dutch on the other page.. I now read from the act of 1910, the first act with respect to aliens, because as you will remember they passed their act before we passed ours. This act was to consolidate and amend the laws with respect to naturalization, and I would like the Secretary of State to listen to section 4 of that act:
Every applicant for naturalization shall:-
(a)	publish in the Gazette a notice, in the 
prescribed form, of his intention to apply for a certificate of naturalization in the union; and
(b)	produce, in support of his application, proof that he has so published such a notice, together with a certificate signed by a magistrate, justice of the peace, or field cornet, stating that the applicant is personally known to the person so signing and that to the best of that person's knowledge and belief the applicant is of good character and repute and possesses the qualifications for naturalization prescribed by this act;
(c)	furnish such further evidence as the minister may require of his service under the crown or (as the case may be) of the period of residence prescribed in the last preceding section as a qualification for naturalization, and of his intention to reside in the union; and
(d)	furnish such evidence as the minister may require as to the name, sex, age, and place of birth of each of his minor children (if any) who, at the time of his application, are-
(i)	resident with him in the union;
(ii)	not resident in the union.
5. The minister, upon receipt of the particulars prescribed in the last preceding section, shall take the applicant's case into consideration and may, with or without assigning any reason, grant or refuse his application as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
I read that because it is one of the standard sections that appeared in all the naturalization acts as drafted by the parliamentary draftsman. Then follow the usual sections with respect to the certifying of the necessary documents.

What is the langugae
qualification there?
It is any langugage which is the official language in the state, I think.

I am sure my hon. friend will admit that this is subject to regulations. The principle of the bill now is that the Secretary of State shall have the discretion of granting or refusing a certificate; and I am sure that obtains in every dominion in the British Empire.

I have mentioned that,
and I say that is the understanding under which this arrangement was arrived at; but I am now stating what are the provisions of the statute in South Africa with respect to the matter, and how proceedings are regulated. There are two questions, one of principle, with which I submit we may not deal without breaking our bargain with Great Britain; and the other the question of procedure, and I am pointing out the requirement of procedure in South Africa which I have just read to the house.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has asked me with respect to the language question.

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett

I am asking you that because it raises another very interesting question with regard to naturalization. My impression is that in South Africa the Dutch language as well as the English language would qualify.

The statutes themselves
are printed, one page in Dutch and the other in English; I have made that clear.

I am pointing out that
a worldwide British naturalization would be granted to a man who could speak only Dutch, in South Africa, but he could not be naturalized in Canada, while in Canada a gentleman who could speak only French may be naturalized but could not be naturalized in South Africa.
Any more senseless remark I have never heard.

If my hon. friend would
only have patience, instead of getting out of temper and describing an hon. gentleman in the terms that he has used, he would have seen in a moment the point which I was trying to make. What we are dealing with after all is British Empire naturalization, and the man who cannot speak-

Will the hon. gentleman
possess his soul in patience?

Then, Mr. Chairman. I
rise to a point of order on the use of the word "senseless."

There is no question of
order, Mr. Chairman. This hon. gentleman has a habit of butting into discussions.

to the hon. gentleman-
I said his observations.

All right, my time will
come.

Mr. Chairman, I have
followed the hon. gentleman very carefully and may I ask a question: In Australia, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa are applications for naturalization referred to the courts?
No.
Oh, oh.

There is not much
sense of humour in that.

Apparently, Mr. Chairman, there are a number of gentlemen who do not desire to follow this question. This is beyond all odds the most important domestic question with which this parliament will deal. I invite gentlemen who are interested in it and 'will take the history of western Canada as an example, to look at the observations which I made in 1914, which were unchallenged and which were regarded at that time by both parties as being sound on a question which engaged the attention of Canadian clubs and other organizations; when all that had to be done was to sign a document before a commissioner or a justice of the peace and post it up; and I saw one member of a legislature wdio was elected by sixteen men, none of whom was able to understand practically a single word in the English or the French language, who could only speak Italian and had to do it through an interpreter. I am only mentioning that to show the seriousness of the matter with which we are dealing.
Now I will deal further with the South African statute. The South African statute to which I refer was that of 1910. which was amended after the war, in 1926; and the South African statute has at least some analogy to the conditions we have here, because they have at least two official languages there, and we have two here. The first section provides that the named persons shall be deemed natural born British subjects. Then follow the provisions for the naturalization of aliens, and subsection (b) of section 2 reads as follows:
That he is of good character and able to read and write-
I hope the hon. gentleman will follow this:
-either of the official languages of the union, to the satisfaction of the minister.
That is the position and it is contained in the last of the South African acts, namely, that of 1926.
The next question which arises in regard to South Africa is: How does the minister satisfy himself upon that point? I find that section 19 of the act deals with the matter in the following terms:
Every applicant for naturalization shall-
(a)	not less than one month before he makes application for naturalization to the minister, publish in the Gazette in both the official languages and in one English and one Dutch newspaper circulating in the district in which ho resides, a notice, in the prescribed form, of his intention to apply under this act for a certificate of naturalization; and
(b)	produce, in support of his application, proof that he has so published such notices together with a certificate signed by a magistrate, or justice of the peace, stating that the person so signing has satisfied himself by in-

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
quiries instituted by him that the applicant is of good character and repute and possesses the qualifications for naturalization prescribed by this act;
(c)	furnish such further evidence as the minister may require of his service under the crown or (as the case may be) the period of his residence prescribed in section two as a qualification for naturalization and of his intention to reside in the union; and
(d)	furnish such evidence as the minister may require as to the name, sex, age, and place of birth of each of his minor children (if any) who, at the time of his application, are-
(1)	resident -with him in the union;
(ii) not resident in the union.
(2)	Any person may on payment of the prescribed fee inspect any document produced under subsection 1 of this section.
Then follows section 20, which states:
Any person may make representations to the minister with regard to any person who has applied or has advertised his intention to apply for naturalization.
(2)	The representations shall be in the form of an affidavit.
(3)	The contents of any affidavit filed with the minister in pursuance of this section shall not be disclosed to any person other than for the purpose of legal proceedings for any false statement made in the affidavit.
Then follow sections 21 and 22, dealing with the evidence of declarations and certificates of naturalization. Then there follows this further provision in section 27:
(1) The minister shall-
(a) enrol as of record the issue of all certificates of naturalization granted under this act;
(b)	cancel all certificates of naturalization which have been revoked and publish in the Gazette a list of such revocations with such details as may be prescribed;
(c) cause to be made indices of all the certificates of naturalization (whether granted under this act or any prior law) and permit any person at all reasonable times to inspect the indices and to make copies of such certificates, on payment of the prescribed fee;
(d)	In the months of January and July in every year, publish in the Gazette a return of all persons to whom certificates of naturalization have been granted during the preceding half-year, and in that return show, in respect of each person-
(i)	his name in full;
(ii)	his birthplace;
(iii)	his nationality prior to the grant of the certificate of naturalization;
(iv)	his occupation;
(v)	the date of the issue of the certificate of naturalization.
I point these out because they are the provisions in the statute of South Africa where they have two official languages, the Dutch and the English, and where the minister may not grant an applicant a certificate of naturalization unless and until the formalities which I have cited have been observed. They are not regulations that may be changed

by order in council but regulations that are part of the statutory law of the country and that are not left to either the whim or the caprice of ministers or governments. That is the position with respect to South Africa.
In the commonwealth of Australia there are with respect to naturalization provisions much the same in terms as those which exist in New Zealand except that, the law having been consolidated in 1920, they are somewhat more ample than they are in this country, or, in fact, than in some others. Division 3 relates to procedure and evidence and this is the way in which they deal with the matter in Australia under section 25 of the act and not by regulations. Section 25 reads:
(1)	An applicant for a certificate of naturalization shall produce in support of his application his own statutory declaration stating his name, age, birthplace, occupation and residence, the length of his residence in the British Empire or the period within the eight years preceding the date of his application during which he has been in the service of the crown, and such other particulars as are prescribed and that he intends to settle in the British Empire or to enter or continue in the service of the crown.
(2)	In addition to compliance with the preceding provisions of this section an applicant shall-	.
(a)	advertise in the manner prescribed lus intention to seek naturalization and produce to the minister newspapers containing copies of the prescribed advertisement; and
(b)	produce certificates of character from three natural-born British subjects, two of whom are householders and one of whom is a justice of the peace, a postmaster, a teacher of a state school or an officer of the police force of the commonwealth or a state.
(3)	Any person may on payment of the prescribed fee, inspect any certificate produced in pursuance of the last preceding subsection.
Then there are the same provisions as in South Africa with respect to the right of any person to make declarations in opposition to the application for naturalization. The statute was amended later by striking out the words " justice of the peace ", but I do not concede that to be of importance to the discussion that we are now having. In 1922 there were certain other amendments that do not touch this point.
What have we? We have first of all an agreement by Great Britain as to naturalization and we were to pass a standard bill throughout the British Empire with respect to principle, the procedure being left largely, if not entirely, to the local authorities except that the several bills seem to have been drafted by the parliamentary draftsman in Great Britain. I have read to the committee the provisions in South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland. When we in Canada came to consider this matter we did

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
not do so in a hurry nor without careful consideration of what was involved. When Mr. Doherty, the then Minister of Justice, moved the first reading of his bill in the House of Commons on the 22nd May, 1914, he explained the circumstances with great fullness to the house. The then leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, made some Observations, and during the course of the debate I thought it desirable to mention what had been going on in western Canada with respect to naturalization and the pressure that was being brought to bear upon public men to ensure a better law and a more wholesome observance of the law as it then stood. For instance, I then placed upon Hansard the circumstances under which naturalization was granted in the United States and the words of the statute are worth while considering. They are these:
That every final hearing upon such petitions shall be had in open court before a judge or judges thereof, and every final order which may be made upon such petition shall be under the hand of the court and entered in full upon a record kept for that purpose, and upon such final hearing of such petition the applicant and witnesses shall be examined under oath before the court and in the presence of the court.
Not only the applicant but the witnesses have to be examined under oath. In the United States the provision with respect to language deals only with the English language, they having but one official language. The provision is this:
That no alien shall hereafter be naturalized or admitted as a citizen of the United States who cannot speak the English language: Provided, that this requirement shall not apply to aliens-
-under certain circumstances that have no bearing on this discussion. The bill passed its second reading, was considered in committee and then came up for third reading in the house. When it came up for third reading on June 4 -and I direct the attention of the Secretary of State to the words of the great leader of the Liberal party in connection with this matter-Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved the following amendment:
That this bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house with instructions that they have power to amend it by striking out subsections 3 and 5 of section 2.
He argued that they should be struck out because they gave too wide powers to the Secretary of State and these are his words which I commend to the minister at this time:
We have given the courts of law the power to determine that question, and we have provided that the applicant must come before
the court and give evidence of his character; that the judge may, if not satisfied with the proof placed before him, ask for further evidence, and that there may be a trial before the judge as to whether or not the applicant is a fit and proper person to be a British subject.
Further he said:
The judge determines the question, and then the matter is not finally disposed of, but is referred to the Secretary of State, who, purely arbitrarily, without giving any reasons, but simply of his own will, may or may not grant a certificate. Such a disposition is absolutely repugnant to the spirit of our institutions.
Those are the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Did that speech convince my hon. friend at the time and did he vote for Sir Wilfrid Laurier's amendment?

He certainly did not
for reasons I can explain to the minister so easily that there will be no difficulty in his understanding this, that the bill in that regard was a standard bill and at the conference that took place in England Mr. Churchill and Sir John Simon stated the position in these words. Mr. Churchill said:
The grant of nationality is in every case discretionary and this discretion should be exercised by those responsible in the area in which the applicant has spent the last twelve months.
This is what Sir John Simon said:
It is essential to the scheme which the Home Secretary lias referred to, that the grant of an imperial certificate should be a matter of discretion, and that that discretion should be exercised, not in all eases by the home government, of course, but by the authority which has the local opportunity of judging of the man's personal qualities and credentials during the last year of his five years. That seems to me to be essential to the scheme.
Therefore the scheme went by the board unless it were adopted as a whole, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier was so taken with the explanation that was given that the amendment of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was negatived on division without any vote being recorded. The point to which I direct attention is that the Liberal party of that day set its face steadily against bureaucracy and centralization, against the usurpation of power by a minister in regard to matters that concern the whole body politic of this country, and where- the exercise of that power improperly would involve very serious consequences to the country. I could have read further, but I have read just that to show what the leader of the opposition at that time said.
But let us go further. Let us look into this matter from the other angle. I have stated the principle and I have stated the procedure of the various countries, but let us

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
ask what we are now doing, because that is the important thing. What we are now doing is at variance with what has been done in communities similarly situated to ours. But we go further than that. This entrusts to the minister, by any machinery that he at his whim may set lip, the determination of the fitness of a man to become a British subject. That is what is does in terms. Why abolish the judicial proceedings? Why abolish the judges? It is said that it means great cost and expense, but what is that compared with the cost and expense in the United States, or in South Africa? What is the cost compared with the priceless boon that is being conferred upon these people by giving them British ctizenship? We have courts in this country, and I would like hon. gentlemen opposite to know that in all the western country, about which they are so solicitous, the county court judges hold their courts in practically every small community of western Canada.
Oh no.

The local government can easily provide that. They do in Alberta. It is only the local government that has authority in that matter, and it has been a Liberal local government in Saskatchewan ever since 1905. If they have not these facilities there it is the fault of the local government, not of this parliament. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) shakes his head. He knows perfectly well that the only authority that may determine the place of the sittings of the court is the provincial government, and if they have not these facilities in his part of the country, it is because they have not been given to the people by the local government. 'But in Alberta, in every small community, the district courts meet from time to time for the purpose of enabling litigants to dispose of small suits up to $600, and will any man in this house say that you can travel a considerable distance to deal with a $100 suit, and not regard it important enough to travel that distance to become a British subject? That is the question.
Let me go further. Think what it means to Great Britain. We are not paying the piper. We are not maintaining a fleet on the high seas that polices the world. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) is not interested in that. They are paying it over yonder, and we owe to them a duty to see to it that we protect this naturalization of ours in every way and manner in which it is possible to do so, in order that the responsibility upon Great Britain may not be greater than it is.
I will tell hon. gentlemen of something I have seen with my own eyes and heard with my own ears. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Glen) and my hon. friend from Yorkton are both members of the same profession to which I belong, and I ask them if during the last ten years they have not been in courts of law in this country in which cases were being carried on in which neither party could give his story in either the English or the French language.
What has that got to do with it?

I thought they would say that. Do they realize that this statute says that a certificate of naturalization shall not be granted to any alien unless he possesses an adequate knowledge of either the English or French language? What has that got to do with it? Simply this, that wherever you see in this country British subjects who have no adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language, you know perfectly well that naturalization has been granted in some wrong and improper manner.

Would they
necessarily have to 'be British subjects if they appeared in a suit in a court of law?
I am unable to understand the question.

I will explain it. The leader of the opposition appealed to two hon. gentlemen on this side belonging to the bar and cited cases in court where the principals could not state their case in either English or French at least leaving us to assume that they must be Canadian citizens, and that somebody had been derelict in his duty in granting naturalization to these people without their possessing an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language.
We will add to it that they were British subjects.
That is different.
That is the point I am making, and if there is any misunderstanding about that, I will remove it at once.
For information, may I ask if the term "Canadian citizen" is used anywhere in the Naturalization Act?

My hon. friend from
Winnipeg South Centre has more time to go over the act than I have, and can find that out for himself.
Let us go a step further. What are you doing in this statute? Perhaps to the hon.

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
gentleman it means nothing, it is perhaps a huge joke that you naturalize by the hundred people who have no adequate knowledge of either the English or French language. I have been in communities' where people had citizenship papers and could not speak either the English or the French language.
If my hon. friend will allow me, is not that evident proof that in such cases the courts did not act properly? That is just what we claim.
Hear, hear.
If hon. gentlemen will just wait a moment, they will not cheer. They were cases under the old act which made no provision for a knowledge of either the English or French language.
Why cite those cases at all, then?

To show what this act means to this country. Great Britain and ourselves made the agreement we did to bring about a uniform law, and in those countries where there was only one official language, the language was to be English, and in those countries where there were two official languages, it could be either English or another official language; but prior to 1914 there were no provisions with respect to any tongue whatsoever, and my hon. friends know that it was a crying scandal in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and partly in Manitoba, where thousands of men were naturalized by being huddled together in a group, and someone going in to them with a paper and asking them to sign their names-

That was under the
Roblin government.

That shows the type of mind of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. He says it was under the Roblin government.	What did they have to do
with naturalization? Surely he knows better than that.

Their friends,
the government of the day in Ottawa, had something to do with it.

From 1911 to 1914 the old statute prevailed, but in 1914 the new act was enacted. Fourteen years have elapsed since then, and wherever you findl a naturalization certificate in the possession of a man under the age of thirty-five in this country- they had to be twenty-one years old to be naturalized, and fourteen years have elapsed since-someone has failed in his duty if that man does not possess an adequate knowledge
of either the English or the French language. What have we seen prior to that time? Prior to 1914 we have seen men huddled together in a group, names signed, a person, usually some heeler, appointed a notary public, a commissioner of oaths or justice of the peace for the purpose, and going in and signing a certificate that these men were of good character, although he had never seen them before, they having been just rushed up to sign the necessary documents, and then certificates were granted-they called them citizenship papers. I have seen these papers with my own eyes in the possession of men in court who were unable to speak either the English or the French language, and who could only communicate through an interpreter. It was to stop that sort of thing that this statute was passed, to compel them to have an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language before they could receive a certificate of naturalization, a certificate, mark you, that gave them British citizenship not merely in Canada, not merely within the three-mile limit, but within every part of the world.
What did we witness during the war? I wonder if hon. gentlemen recall in their own communities what I have seen in mine? I received a letter from a soldier at the front who had seen as a prisoner of war, one who had been a German barber in the city of Calgary a few months before. This man was a naturalized Canadian. Does that mean anything? That is the very sort of thing we want to prevent. He was a German citizen. The moment he got outside the three-mile limit he was no longer a British subject.

It shows that the hon.
member for West Calgary must have had a very close shave.

It may be as amusing
as that to the hon. gentleman; it is not to me. I believe it strikes at the very foundation of the life of this country. I ventured to say so in 1914, and I have a stronger view now than I had then, for I have watched the administration of this law. Let me go one step further. There was a well-known citizen of one of our communities who was naturalized, and yet he was captured within the German lines. On the bodies of some of those who unfortunately met their death in the war there was found evidence of their having been in Canada not very long before.
In 1914 we endeavoured to meet a new situation by this legislation, and we provided the machinery which Sir Wilfrid Laurier said

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
had been in use in this country from the very inception of our form of naturalization. He put it in this way:
When we adopted the law of naturalization, we did not copy the British precedent. We did not provide that' the Secretary of State should arbitrarily have the power which is given to the Home Office in Great Britain; but we provided that the decision of the judge should be final and should not be revised by anyone. I have not heard that any complication has arisen; or that it has ever been felt that there was in Canada any necessity, as there appears to be in Great Britain, for the Secretary of State to be given such power as this.
But he added:
If there is reason for such legislation, it must be that the government of Great Britain have found it necessary, in order to avoid diplomatic complications, to reserve that power.
And after the explanation of Mr. Doherty, the third reading of the bill was given on division, Sir Wilfrid being satisfied by the statement made with respect to the diplomatic obligations that were involved in connection with this imperial citizenship.
Now I ask the minister this question. We have passed principle, we have passed procedure as it is in other countries. What does he propose? He proposes to do one of two things. His amendment provides that the minister must be satisfied. Therefore the minister himself must go and find out personally, or he must delegate the power to someone else; there is no alternative. He is not going to wander over this country and examine each applicant for naturalization to see if he has an adequate knowledge of English or French; he cannot do it personally; therefore he is going to delegate that power to someone. Who is this to be? That is the problem. In times past that power has been delegated to our judges, and to them only, for this reason: there is the machinery-the clerks, the place where notices can be given, the boards on which they can be displayed. In South Africa and other countries these notices are published in the official gazette; here , they are posted on a board in the clerk's office. Again I ask, to whom is he going to delegate that power. Yesterday he said: to homestead inspectors or the mounted police. They are already used by the minister for certain work. But to whom is he going to delegate the power to determine whether these applicants for naturalization have an adequate knowledge of English or French? He read from a letter written by Chief Justice Meredith, who points out that the Secretary of State has given no lead as to how these matters should be determined, and each judge must determine them for himself. That is so.

There is no uniformity decision in matters of judicial discretion. It has been laid down by all the great law lords that while judicial discretion is hedged around by certain rules, and there is no such thing as a casual or whimsical expression of discretion, yet the judicial discretion of one judge may not be the judicial discretion of another. In this case, for instance, one judge might regard a sufficient knowledge of English or French as being indicated by a casual conversation, while another might say: I want you to answer certain questions.
Do hon. gentlemen realize the implications of this measure? We have provided, that the Secretary of State shall be satisfied, and up to this moment we have said that the power is judicial and not political. But a homestead inspector is a political appointee. There was a day in the province of Alberta when homestead inspectors went out to alien settlements holding in the one hand a recommendation for a patent for 160 acres of land and in the other an application for naturalization. That dlay is not so long past, and I speak of wihat I know; it ended in 1911. Then the war came on and now homestead inspectors are appointed under the Civil Service Commission; but everyone knows that the condition to which I have referred did prevail prior to 1911. There were communities of new immigrants in those days, they had been here some three years, and that is the condtion that prevailed. The two things went side by side.
Did that condition cease in 1911?
I cannot say very much about that except in my own community.
It operated in 1926.

Absolutely.
M'r. BENNETT: The Minister of Railways says it operated in 1926.
My hon. friend put on special homestead inspectors in 1926 and paid them for two months.
I am glad that has been mentioned. I was Acting Minister of the Interior at the time, and found that a number of special homestead inspectors had been appointed by the minister. I continued them.
By what minister?

By the Hon. Charles
Stewart, Minister of the Interior. What is more, I can give the names if the hon. gentleman will allow me sufficient time. The superintendent, was a man named Cuttle, I think.

May I ask the hon. member a question?
One of them went down to Moose Jaw, I suppose that is what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) wishes to ask about.

It may be there were six. When the Minister of Railways says the same thing happened in 1926 he is stating what is incorrect, and he must know it to be incorrect.
No.
I challenge him to name any case where a homestead inspector went into any community with certificates of naturalization in one hand and recommendations for patents in the other.

My hon. friend a moment before was speaking about a homestead inspector having it in his power to make a recommendation as to whether or not an individual should get 160 acres of land. I say that men were put on specially in 1926, when my hon. friends were in power, in order to exercise that power to the full for political purposes.	.

Once more the Minister of Railways does the same old trick. He heard my statement perfectly well, that prior to 1911 homestead inspectors went into settlements of aliens with applications for naturalization in one hand and in the other recommendations for patents for homesteads, and he said the same thing prevailed in 1926. I say no; they had no power after 1914 to do that.

I asked if that condition continued after 1911 till 1914, and the hon. leader of the opposition was dealing with my question in relation to his own district. It was then that the Minister of Railways got into the discussion.
Exactly.
That is right.

My hon. friend spoke of the condition in Moose Jaw. The three men who were temporarily appointed
in Moose Jaw were dismissed, and six new men were put on in their place. One of them never made a report on any homestead entry throughout the whole time he was supposed to be engaged on such work; instead, he used the money to travel around constituencies in southern Saskatchewan for political purposes.

All right. Now having
heard the question of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, it reminds me of the mounted police brought from Toronto to Regina in 1925 to vote for the government,
What about the mounted police sent from Regina to the Klondike?

An officer was sent from
Regina to the Klondike upon the recommendation of Commissioner Starnes. It is there in black and white and I saw it with my own eyes.

I cannot say; I do not
know. Let us get down to the Naturalization Act again. I confess to having a great interest in this matter. Prior to 1911 I travelled considerably throughout western Canada to ascertain what had been done under our Naturalization Act. I did not confine myself to the province of Alberta; I went to Saskatchewan. I went into districts that had been settled by men who came from lands outside the British Empire and I found that these men had been naturalized. I found also that they had no knowledge of either English or French. I was quite anxious about the act of 1914, and I am free to say that I discussed the matter not only with my own party leaders but with other gentlemen who were vastly more interested in the welfare of Canada and of the British Empire than they were in the political fortunes of their own party. And there are, strange as it may sound, such gentlemen on the Liberal side in this country. They were vastly more interested, I say, in this matter than they were in their own political welfare, and so when the question came before the House of Commons embodying this legislation that had been decided upon, Sir Wilfrid Laurier congratulated the then Minister of Justice. Mark you, Sir Wilfrid Laurier who was dealing with the matter, after the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty had made his speech, following that gentleman immediately, pointed out that the matter had been engaging the attention of successive governments and that he was very glad that they had been able to get the legislation

through. Mr. Martin-later Chief Justice Martin-also spoke after Mr. Macdonald of Pict.ou had addressed the house. Let me quote the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
I am sorry that I was called away during the very interesting address of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and that, therefore, I missed part of what he said. The chief object of this bill is to deal with the effect of the certificate of naturalization which is given in any one of the dominions of the empire. That is very important legislation, which has been in contemplation for many years, and I am very glad that my hon. friend has at last achieved the making of these provisions.

Again, I was going to ask the one question which I think must appeal to the Secretary of State: How is he to be informed in order to exercise hi3 discretion? It is admitted that be can do it only in one of two ways, either directly by going himself, or indirectly by sending someone else. And whom have we sent heretofore? The judges of the country.
How is the Secretary of State in South Africa or New Zealand or Australia informed?

I am suggesting that there is another way of doing it, namely, by the production of evidence from two witnesses, naming and describing them in terms'. But we thought it easier and simpler, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier recognized, that the judges should determine whether or not the conditions' imposed by the statute had been observed. What are these qualifications? They are these three-let hon. members bear them in mind: residence, character, language. Residence of five years, good character, and, lastly, an adequate knowledge of either English or French.
These remain in the act.

But how does the Secretary of State satisfy himself in the matter? Can any homestead inspector or any member of the mounted police satisfy himself, as well as a judge can, of the question of residence?
An affidavit does it.
No; the man must appear in person before the judge.

Sometimes they say that truth can be found even in an affidavit.
|Mr. BENNETT:	I have not practised
among the class of persons to whom that remark applies. The man, I say, appears in person; that is the essential thing. In South Africa, my hon. friend from Yorkton says, he does not apear in person; in the gazette notice is given to the world, and two persons by affidavit give their evidence, and in addition to that there is another certificate required. Thereafter the minister may act. At the present time in Canada what happens? The judge makes his report. If hon. gentlemen have ever attended a court in this country and witnessed naturalization proceedings they will appreciate the importance of the question, Hon. gentlemen of the legal profession have no doubt done so.

It is a most perfunctory thing. The evidence is supplied by the mounted police, and it can be supplied under the new legislation. The party can go before a mounted police officer and make affidavit, and the officer can find out whether he can speak English or French. The whole thing is sent to the Secretary of State, avoiding the cost of appearance before the court.
My hon. friend says that the applicant goes before the mounted police. Is it any more difficult to go before a judge?
The mounted police officer visits him at his house.
Then it is a peripatetic court that visits the applicant?
Precisely. That is what is done, in Montreal at any rate.
I cannot think that in Montreal the Secretary of State is issuing certificates in regard to which there is no judicial recommendation.
Not at all. But I say that the information which the judge obtains is obtained largely from the mounted police.
That is, as to character.
The man appears before the judge, who looks at him. How can the judge tell what kind of character he has by merely looking at him?

If this is to be an experience meeting I will give my experience. Within the last eighteen months I have witnessed the proceedings with respect to an application. The man appeared in court, having given his notice. It took place in the supreme court. The judge tested his ability to speak in either English or French, putting

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
various questions to him. He admitted that he knew no French, stating where he had come from. The judge then tested his knowledge of English. He went further. He inquired as to the man's attitude towards government: he asked him whether he knew anything of the Bolshevik movement, the man having come from Russia. Certain other questions were also asked as to what the man read, his literature, the documents he had been receiving, what people had visited him, and so forth. The judge took a great deal of pains in the matter. He then had evidence given, by affidavits, it is true, although the parties were there to be called, if necessary, as to character. Then the question of residence was considered, evidence being given not only by the man himself but, as well, by others. The judge made his report. It was quite apparent that the applicant in one case-there were several of them-had no knowledge of English or French and the judge declined to make the recommendation. That is my recollection of what occurred.
How could the judge converse with him?

The court interpreter
was there.

That gave the thing away at
once.

Now, this idea of railroading British citizens through-using the term railroading in the sense in which it was employed by an hon. gentleman in this house yesterday-is something to be deprecated. Hon. gentlemen may regard this matter lightly as something to be treated casually. For my part it is the most serious question we have considered this session or shall have considered for years to come. That at any rate is my personal view. The hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) may be fortunate in coming from a city, but I put this to him: If British citizenship is worth anything why should not the man in Montreal be prepared to go to the court?

Why have two forums?
Either go before a judge and get naturalized or obtain naturalization from the Secretary of State. But why two jurisdictions?

The Secretary of State
can grant it only if he refers the matter to a judge. But at his discretion, in extraordinary cases, he may grant it without such a reference. And it may be that cases which so eminent a lawyer as my hon. friend urges the Secretary of State to treat as extraordinary are so treated. But that comes back to the point I am making, that the matter be-56103-162
comes a political question, which it ought not to be. The hon. member has proved it now, in his own experience.

I may tell "my hon. friend
that when I sat on the other side of the house I used practically the same arguments as he is now advancing, though not so volubly. I pointed out that I had no confidence in the Secretary of State under any Conservative government, and consequently I would vote against the legislation. Since that time I have changed my mind.

Well, I must say that
since the hon. gentleman is so frank I am satisfied when the people of this country read his observations they will be a unit in opposition to this present legislation.

I think I owe it to my
hon. friend to say that.

I cannot think my hon.
friend owes it to himself or to the Secretary of State to say it, because I cannot think it highly creditable to either. But let us go a step further. The hon. gentleman has said that he is going to substitute homestead inspectors or mounted police or some other source of information for the courts. If he is not going to do it himself who is going to do it for him?

Since my hon. friend did not speak on the second reading, I was endeavouring to let him present his argument as much as possible in an orderly manner and without interruption. If it is so desired, later on I will explain fully the machinery of the department, but I would remind my hon. friend that now in every case the Secretary of State makes inquiry, and it has often happened that, although the courts have recommended a certificate, or in the language of Chief Justice Meredith have not thought it their duty to oppose an application, on our own information we have refused to grant the certificate. In many cases we have proved harder to satisfy than the courts as to the qualifications of applicants, and my hon. friend from Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) made a good point a moment ago when he said that when the court desires to have a naturalization case heard, it appeals to us for evidence. We produce our own evidence before the court, which is a rather extraordinary proceeding, but I would point out that in a number of cases the courts have railroaded through twenty-five or fifty naturalization cases in a few moments, simply disregarding the hearing of them because they take it for granted that we will inquire into them and do our own work.

The judges of the community where I live do not treat these cases in that way, but it is possible that my hon. friend is right so I must accept his statement.
My position is simply this, and I have concluded:	You have your principle, which is
universal throughout the empire, varied only by the offijcial languages of the country in which the application is made. You have your procedure, which varies from declarations and affidavits to notices in gazettes and newspapers supported by witnesses in courts or by declarations, but in any event evidence which satisfies |the minister and upon which he acts. Heretofore in this country we have said that the evidence upon which the minister must act is the judicial report plus independent inquiries. We are now abrogating the provisions with respect to judicial inquiries; we are wiping them out entirely and making it unnecessary for the applicant to attend in court. We are doing away with the publicity which attaches to that, appearance in court, and I would remind hon. gentlemen that in the United States a great deal of importance is attached to that appearance. If any hon. members have seen an application for naturalization in an United States court they will remember the ceremony which is gone through, the reverence and love for the flag, teaching Americanism right on the threshold of the application. The way in which this is done is most astounding; the flag is sometimes produced and an explanation is given by the judge; there is the appearance of the applicant and of the two witnesses. Then in the morning papers there will be a heading, "New citizens made", with a full announcement of the proceedings.
As the bill now before us stands, practically all the safeguards which exist in other countries are done away with, because in most the procedure is provided by statute as distinguished from the mere whim of the minister. My friend the Secretary of State has commanded the confidence of the hon. member for Cartier, but it is not the individual of whom we are speaking; it is the office as such. With the pressure of business and with the other difficulties in the way, how is the minister able to review these matters? Very often it gets down to being done by some clerk, who produces the file and says, " It is all ready to sign " and the minister signs it. I ask the minister here and now how many of these files he has read through since assuming office; if he has read them through, he is the only minister to have done so within my knowledge. What happens at present is that the testimony is placed
[Mr. Rinfret.J
on file together with the judicial report, but as it is intended to amend the act that will be the case no longer. Some clerk will determine the question of naturalization in this country by reading those reports. WThat usually happens is that the judge may recommend that a man should not become naturalized, in which case the application is not granted. Or perhaps the judge recommends that a man should become naturalized; this recommendation is supported by testimony from the police and other officials stating that his character is all right, and that ends the whole matter. The second essential, a knowledge of French or English, is where most applications fall down; there has been no adequate inquiry with respect to that matter. Hon. members will remember the letter from Chief Justice Meredith, in which he said these men were illiterate and had no knowledge of our language at all. He is an eminent judge and his duty was clear; he should have said, " No, I cannot recommend this application because there has not been compliance with one of the three conditions." Each of these requirements is equally important; it must be remembered that there is no distinction between them. Whenever anyone meets a man or woman-not so much in the case of women, who do not become naturalized so frequently-under thirty-five years of age, or for the sake of argument we will say thirty-seven or forty years of age, who has become naturalized but who cannot speak either English or French, then the law has been disregarded. You cannot get away from that fact; the law has been disregarded, and because of that fact I have ventured to bring this matter so strongly before the committee. I say this is not the time to relax the safeguards which we have had set up as matters of procedure ever since, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, we have dealt with naturalization at all, in order that each one of these requirements should be dealt with in accordance with the demand made by Chief Justice Meredith when he said, " I sought for guidance from the Secretary of State, but I did not get it." That is the way he put it, as the minister will remember. Chief Justice Meredith asked for some ruling as to what principle should govern in settling these matters, and the ruling is so simple; the Secretary of State should send a circular to all judges stating that under the provisions of the act they are called upon to determine whether or not the applicant has complied with the three conditions by which he may obtain British citizenship: First, has he resided five years in Canada, as provided by the statute; second, has he an adequate knowl-

edge of the English or French language, and third, has he a good character? If the judge cannot report upon these questions it is his duty to sit until he is able to secure such evidence as may be necessary to enable him to make a proper recommendation.

The imputation of bad motives, or motives different from those acknowledged, misrepresenting the language of another, or accusing him, in his turn, of misrepresentation, charging him with falsehood or deceit; or contemptuous or insulting language of any kind; all these are unparliamentary and call for prompt interference.

The hon. member for Cartier has just cited the laws of the outposts of the empire, as he called them, of Newfoundland and New Zealand, to strengthen his argument that it is not really necessary for the applicant to go before a judge, and yet in the same breath he said that we should make laws for ourselves and not concern ourselves with what was done in the other dominions. That is precisely what we did when this act was passed in 1914. We expressly put upon that statute the procedure which should be followed before the application came to the minister for his certificate of naturalization.
The Secretary of State seems to hold the view that he may grant a certificate of naturalization directly under section 4. but that contention, I think, cannot possibly hold. Section 4 gives the qualifications which one must have before he can be granted naturalization papers, and sections 22 to 28, which are now sought to be repealed, say that the minister may grant naturalization only after a certain procedure has been followed. So no application can be made direct to the minister under section 4; it must go through the procedure authorized by the statute, that is, through the court, and from the court to the minister himself. The hon. Secretary of State says that he does not like that double jurisdiction. I should think that in an important matter of this kind, the double or checking jurisdiction of the minister, super-imposed upon the court order, is a very good thing; in fact, the minister has told us already that he has had occasion to apply that provision with very good results, and it is a very useful provision that the minister have the final say as to whether a naturalization certificate shall be granted, no matter what the court has said.
The Secretary of State has said that the intention was to give him this power, but that parliament by putting in this procedure had taken away the power from him. That cannot be. This procedure is too explicit; these provisions mean exactly what they say. The provision that the minister may grant the naturalization certificate in his own discretion is contained in section 4, it is true, but when you come to section 27, you will find that that same provision as to the minister s absolute discretion is contained in the procedure sections. So it was never intended by our
statute to do otherwise than to say, in conformity with the general agreement between the dominions of the empire and the mother country, the Secretary of State in each dominion shall actually issue the certificate of naturalization, thus standing by our bargain with the other dominions. But this parliament in 1914 said: That is not to be the sole test, but the procedure that we are now outlining in the statute is to be carried through, and carried through expressly. The Secretary of State may issue a certificate only when an application therefor has gone through the prescribed channel.
The question arises, what are we going to substitute for that, and there I think the 'Secretary of State is in difficulty. He has nebulous ideas about how the matter is to be carried out, but I judge that he will issue a questionnaire or have agents of some sort, scattered all over this dominion who will collect the information and give a certificate, the information being returned to the Secretary of State. Now can that be as good as having that information gathered and adjudicated upon by the judiciary of the country? We have a judiciary which is held in respect from east to west, and we have placed this particular question in their hands; but now the Secretary of State seeks to substitute local people, homestead inspectors, for instance, and I do not know what other classes, to deal with naturalization. I do not see how that can possibly be a change for the better.
I think there is some merit in the point mentioned by the minister, that there is a certain amount of inconvenience, particularly in the west, on the part of applicants for naturalization getting in touch with the proper officials, but surely those who have charge of the administration of the act, can facilitate applicants getting to the judge or the judge to them. It is a matter of detail and, to my mind, not of sufficient importance to offset the obligation that is upon us so to legislate that the right of British citizenship shall mean something to the person to whom it is granted, and shall be safeguarded most carefully. It entails a responsibility on him to whom it is granted, but particularly on ourselves and on Great Britain, for we have to look to Great Britain for the protection of our citizens abroad. Therefore we should not load this obligation on to the mother country without exercising the greatest possible care.
In the city from which I come many persons apply for naturalization. So far we have had no difficulty, and I think the law has worked out pretty well. By far the majority of those who seek naturalization are of the

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Adshead) has to my mind touched upon what is perhaps the weakest point in the whole legislation as proposed to-day. The Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret), in bringing in the proposed amendment to the act, emphasized the fact that we are basing this law upon the naturalization laws as they exist in other parts of the British Empire. I do not think that we need necessarily copy other portions of the empire, particularly when conditions differ, as they do differ so radically, in different sections of the British Empire. For example, England at the present time is a free trade, or practically, a free trade country; and even the Liberal party in Canada does not advocate free trade on the ground that England has adopted that policy. Similarly, in different parts of the British Empire to-day, conditions are so radically different in regard to the constituent elements of population that, in my opinion, it is unnecessary that our various laws should be identical in the various parts of the commonwealth.
I made it my business this morning to look up some facts touching the subject under discussion, particularly with reference to persons, in the different parts of the empire, who speak neither English nor French-taking English and French in Canada, or English and Dutch in the case of South Africa, although I did not get any details with respect to the latter country. It will illustrate my point better than any words of mine can do, and disclose the situation exactly as it is, if I submit certain figures I have been able to obtain. I take the figures. with regard to Australia and Canada. In New South Wales the population in 1921 numbered 2,101,000. Of that population the English speaking proportion totalled 2,082,000, or 98 per cent. The whole population of Australia, including New South Wales, for the same year, is given as 5,435,000; and to my surprise the proportion of non-British-persons born neither in Australia nor in any other part of the empire-is' given as 50,000-in fact, to be precise, 45,000 odd. In other words, the population of Australia, taken as a whole, is
given as 99 per cent British and only about 1 per cent speaking other languages.
Would those two sets of figures agree? The 2 per cent in the case of New South Wales would be 40,000, and the total for Australia is only 50,000, including the 40,000 non-British in New South Wales.
In New South Wales the number of non-British is 19,000, and for all Australia-I am not giving the figures to the last decimal-50,000 including the 19,000.
I understood you to say 98 per cent.

I gave that figure, though I think it is higher* than that. It probably works out at 99 per cent. I took their own figures from the Statesmen's Year Book, which is a good enough authority for most of us. The total for all Australia, of British born, is 99 per cent. Taking Canada on the other hand we find that the population in this country in 1921 was 8,788,000, and of these the English, Scotch, Irish and French numbered 7,279,000. Because of this difference, and the difference in conditions, I say again that we need not of necessity frame our law to conform exactly to the law of Australia, for example. Let me give some more figures to illustrate the difference in conditions as between Australia and this country. Immigration to Australia in the year 1926 totalled 105,918, and of that number 90,562, or 87 per cent, were British. Unfortunately I had not time enough to look up the figures in regard to Canada, but my recollection is that our immigration in that year would include only about 35 per cent British. I do not wish to be misquoted or misunderstood in this matter. I have great respect- indeed, if I may say so, even affection-for these new Canadians who are coming to our country. I have lived all my life in a section where there are thousands of these "new" Canadians. This is an expression which a friend of mine uses and I rather like it. These people who come from different parts of Europe to live amongst us are admirable and in most cases their children have become very good Canadians. I have practised for upwards of twenty years among them in my profession, and many of them are friends of mine. In fact, I have a large number of friends of all nationalities-Italians, Slovaks, Greeks, Finlanders, Ukrainians, Jews, Hungarians and others from continental Europe. I repeat, they are people for whom I have a very great respect and a real friendship. And, I may add, most of them when they become naturalized vote for me. So that I am not complaining-[DOT]
Does that account for your affection?

Partly, I admit. Possibly I might not respect them quite so much if they did not. They have demonstrated a good brand of intelligence in voting as they do. But there is this to be remembered- and I say it after emphasizing my genuine friendship for these people; for this is not a political subject, as I have said on many occasions on different platforms. It is essential in this country of ours, that if people are to know our customs, to understand our laws and to vote intelligently they should be able to speak either English or French, one of the two official languages of Canada. I submit, therefore, that it is unwise to make naturalization so easy-as this proposed legislation would undoubtedly tend to do-as to remove the incentive for strangers from Eur-

ope and elsewhere to endeavour to acquire a knowledge of either English or French, which is imperative before they can become really good citizens. It is only common sense to expect that people coming to Canada should, before they are given the right to take part in the election of representatives, know something of one of the official languages of the country. They should at least have gained some facility in either English or French in order to understand our laws and to judge intelligently of the questions upon which they are to vote.
I also feel that it is a great privilege and even a blessing to be a Canadian citizen; I sometimes point out to my boys that one of the things for which they can feel grateful, although they had no control over it, is that they were born on the northern half of this continent. I believe it is a real blessing to any young man to know that he was born in Canada. I say this with no disrespect to those great cultured, classical countries of Europe, but I do feel that our opportunities, our broad-minded citizenship, our great advantages in every way, our resources and so on, with all the chances for a young man to go ahead, should make him grateful for having been born in Canada.
