to which my attention has been drawn:
The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the minister, and he may, \vith or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
That simply emphasizes the point I was making. However, to carry on with my argument, I do not know of any reason why there should not be a reasonable delay in granting naturalization to any new citizen of our country. I looked up the United States law to-day, and I found that in that country an alien must declare under oath, before the courts, his intention to become a United States citizen two years before he is permitted to become a citizen. If the United States are so particular that they place a man on probation for two years, surely we should be reasonably careful.
The applicant must apply within three years of his entering the country, and at the end of five years he gets his papers.

But if, during those two
years, he should turn out to be a criminal or
unsuitable for citizenship for one reason or another, the opportunity to lay that fact before the proper officials in the United States is much greater than in Canada, particularly under this proposed amendment.
Supposing he committed a crime after the three year period; how could you safeguard against that?
I do not follow my hon. friend. Does he mean if the applicant committed a crime during the two years of probation?
Yes.

Then they would probably refuse him citizenship, and quite rightly so.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me emphasized what I think is the weak point in the whole proposition, and that is the point to which I object: We are putting in the hands of the Secretary of State, whether of this government or of some future government, powers which would permit him to go very far. I am going to speak quite frankly; these powers would give him the opportunity, before an election for example, to enfranchise for political purposes, thousands of voters in this country who prdbably should not be enfranchised, if he were unscrupulous enough to do so, and he could probably decide a number of seats in that way. That is the danger of the whole proposition, and personally I do not want to put that power in the hands of my friend the present Secretary of State, nor do I want to put it in the hands of a Secretary of State from the Conservative party or from the Progressive party, with all due respect to their probity. I wanted to make this clear, because this is the weakness I see in the whole thing. Last night, when the minister sat down, I asked him a question, and the following remarks were made:
Mr. Manion:	Just before the minister closes
I should like to ask him a question. Under the new system how long would it take for naturalization papers to go through?
Mr. Rinfret:	There would be no definite
time; that would rest with the department.
Mr. Manion:	It could be done immediately?
Mr. Rinfret:	Yes. I thank my hon. friend
for this question, because in a certain number of cases it has proven a great inconvenience that the department has been unable to grant a certificate to qualified persons simply because of the delay of three months which is provided in the present act, and because of the necessity of referring the matter to the courts.
The minister made that very clear, and it is just what I thought he would say. By the proposed amendment, upon receiving a
Naturalization Act

hurried application from any constituency in this country-from the constituency of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, for example, although knowing him as well as I do and haying such a high respect for him I am sure he would not do anything of the kind-the Secretary of State could immediately issue a certificate. I submit that he should not have that right.

My hon. friend has singled me out, but I would point out to him that by speaking of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier he might very well mean his friend Mr. Patenaude, who was candidate in the constituency of Jacques Cartier.
He is not the member for Jacques Cartier, unfortunately. However, I did refer in a jocular way to my hon. friend-
I can quite understand how that rankles in the mind of my hon. friend.

I apologize to my hon. friend, as he is 'the member for Cartier not Jacques Cartier. But I think there will be no mistake as to who was meant. At any rate, I repeat that any member of this house or any candidate for membership in this house might apply for the naturalization of a group of new arrivals in this country just before election time, and I do not believe the power to immediately grant those certificates should be put in the hands of any Secretary of State, whether he is a Conservative, a Liberal or a Progressive. I do not believe human nature is so perfect that, on many occasions under the pressure of candidates running in a tight constituency, the secretary of state of one party or another would not, to put it mildly, stretch a point to grant naturalization. I well remember evil conditions in a certain district in this country, which I do not wish to name because I have no desire to reflect on someone who is gone. In that district there existed the condition described by my hon. leader this afternoon. Years ago when I was a boy I saw hundreds of men who could not speak the English language being naturalized just before an election and given a vote-for no other purpose than that of voting for the gentleman who was a candidate of the government then in power, and who counted upon getting a majority from them to take him back into office.
I do not think it is just to any secretary of state to give him this power. I warn the minister that if this act goes through and he is Secretary of State when the next election comes round he will be driven absolutely crazy by the demands of candidates in various

sections of this country to naturalize large numbers of people who cannot speak the English language, or the French language, people who at the time should not get naturalization papers. Suppose, for example, in a certain constituency, say in my own-and I do not pretend to be any better than anybody else-I am running in a tight election, and there are thousands in that constituency who have come from continental Europe. The larger number of them, we will say, cannot when they first come here speak the English language. Suppose I am unscrupulous enough to have my agent go to them and say: There is a large number of your people here; if you will vote right I will see that you get your naturalization papers at once and it will cost you nothing. Suppose that proposition is put up to a few hundred of them. We get a lot of people in our country who do not understand the language, and the proposition may be explained to them by an interpreter who gives it whatever colouring he pleases. Does my hon. friend think many of them would not accept the suggestion and do that without being dishonest? They have got away from war-ridden Europe, and most of them-those who have not gone across to the states-do want to become Canadians. There are advantages in having Canadian citizenship, and they would largely accept, with no ill feeling; and the only thing that they would be taught by my agent, in all probability, if I were unscrupulous enough to do such a thing, wTould be where they were to put the cross on the ballot. I repeat that I do not believe that power should be given to any secretary of state. We should leave the law as it is, so that the applicant for naturalization must go through the courts as he has to do now, w'ithout any great trouble. He pays, of course, a small fee.
I may add that I have had no complaints among the thousands of Europeans whom I have in my constituency. I looked, while listening to my leader, through the list of the nearly 17,000 who according to this report were granted naturalization in the last year, and I find on nearly every page someone from my own city of Fort William. I did not even know that they were getting it. In an odd case I have been approached to help them through, because for some reason they had been held up by the courts. Generally I have told them to go and- see a lawyer and he would help to get it through. Perhaps a couple of hundred or possibly twice that number in this list were from my own city of Fort W7illiam. I repeat that I wish to protest as strongly as I can against changing this lawr and putting it in the hands of a secretary

Naturalization Act
of state, whether this secretary of state or another, to grant just before an election naturalization to hundreds of thousands of people who perhaps should not be enfranchised. I submit that if that is done, if the law is changed, then within a few years, perhaps in the lifetime of the present Secretary of State or of myself, we will have a scandal which will equal that of the customs scandal of a few years ago. I hope that the Secretary of State and his government will reconsider the whole matter and leave in the courts the duty of handling it, as the courts are a fair and non-political forum.

I have frequently complained to the house and to the minister about the difficulty, the trouble and expense to which my constituents have been put in order to get naturalization. Perhaps I might explain that my district is a new one; the northern part of it is poorly served with railway facilities. These people going to the judicial centres must travel on a train which runs only three times a week. If they remain over one day at the judicial centre, they will miss the train back, and in most cases that means five days away from home and a good deal of trouble and expense.
It may be asserted that a Canadian certificate of naturalization is something which should be prized so highly that it is well worth all this trouble and expense, but the outlay of $25, $30 or $40, which it means to these people, is a great deal more than most of us here would consider. The class of whom I refer are people from the continent of Europe who have come in there without a dollar and have settled on the poorer bush homesteads, they are not people who handle very much money, and the expenditure of $25 or $30 means as much to them as perhaps a thousand dollars would to the average man within the sound of my voice. Most of them have not sufficient food or clothing in their houses, and nothing in the way of comfort, and this expenditure is something which they cannot well afford. My objection is not particularly to the fact that they must appear before a judge. In all these years, with all the complaints I have heard from these people, I have never heard one of them complain of the fact that they have been obliged to appear before a judge. I think they are satisfied so far as that is concerned, but the difficulty is in getting to the judge; and frequently, in addition to what I have already said, when they get there they find the court is postponed or their own case is set back for
another hearing, and they must repeat their journey two or three times in succession until their application is finally passed or rejected, as the case may be.

May I ask the hon. gentleman if there would not be the same procedure and delays if it were being done through the Department of the Secretary of State? Somebody has to be there to meet them and ask them questions, and -they have to meet somewhere.

I do not know what
the Secretary of State has in mind, but I think the suggestion of the mounted police going out and meeting these people would do away with a good deal of trouble. If my hon. friend will allow me to proceed, I think I can make my meaning clear in a moment. I have discussed this at intervals with the Secretary of State, who is making an honest endeavour to get around the difficulty. The fact has been referred to that the judges meet at various llocal points, and that is true; and in many of the parts where most of my people live the judge will come probably one day a year. In the village in which I reside, the judge comes but one day a year. If we could have these outstanding applications examined at that point, or at these different points on the day on which the judge is there, there would be no difficulty at all, and I would have no objection to the present law. That is what I have tried to secure and what I have discussed frequently with the Secretary of State and with the Under Secretary of State. Indeed I discussed the matter with a member of the -bench and I was told that no provision is made for the extra expenses of judges and that in most cases this would necessitate a judge remaining over another day. In my particular village the judge comes in on one train which gets there in the evening, holds court at night, finishes up his cases and goes back to the judicial centre the next morning. He will not remain over the next day because that would mean two days on account of the train service and ordinarily he refuses to examine these parties in the list of cases on his docket. I suggested to the minister that the department should provide the necessary expenses to enable the judge to remain over another day, but it was pointed out to me again that the judges are under the control of the provincial authorities and that this was something over which the Department of Secretary of State had no jurisdiction whatever.
Those are many of the difficulties that I have met in trying to get some arrangement that would be satisfactory to the people of my

Naiiirilization Act
district. Perhaps the grievance is more a question of administration than one of legislation and I think it can easily be remedied. An hon. member suggests to me that the difficulty might be met by a change in the law in regard to rural districts; that is, to provide some other machinery than the court for examinations in the rural districts and to leave the Iqw as it stands in regard to the cities. Naturally there is no expense or no difficulty for anyone applying for Canadian naturalization to appear before a judge in a city. The difficulty is, as I stated, in these remote rural districts where a trip of five or six days, perhaps repated two or three and sometimes four times, is involved. What happens very frequently when an outsider finds himself up against so many difficulties is that he simply drops the matter altogether and does not bother about it further, and it is desirable for us to induce these people to become naturalized Canadian citizens.
A constituent of mine pointed out to me the difficulty that he was up against. I think I read his letter in the house four or five years ago. He said: "I am making an honest attempt to become a naturalized Canadian citizen. I realize at the same time that the moment I take out papers of naturalization I am taking the resposibility on myself and putting the responsibility on my children, because if another war breaks out my boys are liable to be conscripted but my neighbours"-and he mentioned several-"have not bothered about the matter." In the last war these people, although they have been resident in Canada for many years, were not subject to the conscription law simply because they had not bothered to take out naturalization certificates. I am just pointing out what one of these aliens thought about the matter. He was only endeavouring to do his duty in taking out Canadian papers and it appeared to him that we were putting many stumbling blocks and difficulties in his way.
Further, I am not in favour of the present measure that we are discussing. I agree almost entirely with what the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has said; I can see the same objection, but I ask the committee to give some sympathetic consideration to those people who live in remote districts, who handle only a matter of a few dollars in a year and to whom twenty-five or thirty dollars of an expenditure means a great deal when they are short of the very necessities of life in their own homes. If some extension of funds can be made to the judges to enable

them to stop over another day at these local points throughout the judicial district, the objection will be met. Those people, as I say, have no objection to the present system so far as going before a judge is concerned. I have not heard a single complaint about that. Any man who goes to the trouble of making an application for naturalization is naturally prepared to go to some further trouble. He knows that the must comply' with certain conditions in order to secure Canadian citizenship; but as I pointed out, the difficulties are frequently so great that he gives up in disgust.
Another source of a good deal of grievance is that applicants are frequently called upon to attend court in judicial centres during the threshing season. I have found that in dozens and dozens of cases men have been summoned to appear before a judge right in the middle of threshing when they cannot possibly go. The result is that the application is cancelled, the five dollar fee is lost, and they must make out a new set of papers, pay a new fee, and go through all routine again. Therefore there are many difficulties that we ought to relieve them of so far as possible.
I agree with what the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has said about the political influence to which the minister wiil be subjected if we allow this bill to go through in its present form. There should be some time limit during which notices should be filed in the office of the county court clerk, the post office, the provincial gazette, the local paper or somewhere else before the application can be considered; otherwise, as hon. members have said, you will simply leave the door open and subject the minister to all kinds of political influences on the eve of an election. While I have every confidence in the integrity and honesty of the present minister, if he will not give in to that sort of pressure he is more than human, he is a different type of man from the rest of us. It is not fair to the house to leave any minister subject to that pressure; it is not fair to the minister to leave the door open to subject himself or any succeeding minister to that kind of pressure, and I appeal to him to make some changes in the legislation to meet the objections which I have stated and to provide that the application shall be left on file for some reasonable time before it can be dealt with. I think the suggestion that was made by the leader of the opposition, copied from the system in use in South Africa, was a very

Naturalization Act
good one, namely, that the application should be advertised in a local paper for a matter of three or four or six months and that copies of that paper must be produced before a certificate of naturalization is granted. I appeal to the minister to take some of these matters into consideration and to alter the present legislation to meet these objections without making it as drastic in its application as the proposed amendment now before the committee.

I fail to see where the government has any mandate to bring in this particular legislation. I come from a district where there are six county court judges who administer the Naturalization Act well. The judges are making an application as a body for an increase in salary and in the special committee dealing with the matter further the county court judges who come from the west speak in high terms of the present statute tand its administration. For instance, Judge Jackson says that it is one of the most important parts of the judicial duties to examine applicants who come before him for naturalization and to find out if they have proper ideals of citizenship. A person may become a British subject in two ways: first, by birth, and second, by naturalization. Ever since confederation the question of naturalization has caused a great deal of trouble in parliament. As I say the government has no mandate on this particular question and no complaints have been made that the act is not working out satisfactorily. It seems to me that this is a nice little gesture to certain interests in the west and that the present change is more a matter of politics and political expediency than of policy or laws. The present act as a matter of policy is an essential.' The Anglican church and the Presbyterian church represent a large body of opinion in this country. I cannot speak for them but I wish to refer to what has been said by them at their various synods and assembles. The Anglicans at the general synod at Kingston were alarmed at the aggression of foreigners in Canada and the catering to them by governments. They are beginning to doubt in view of the alarming immigration figures, whether Canada is going to continue to be a British country. Look at the situation in the United States. When President Harding found by the last census that the United States had only about 53 or 54 per cent of American-bom citizens, they decided to dose their doors to immigration from continental Europe, and they established their quota system, and that is what Canada will come to sooner or later. This country
is at the parting of the ways to-day, with the repeal of the sedition clause in the criminal code and this repeal now.
This is a political bill, Mr. Chairman, and it was never intended to be anything else. It is a nise gesture to the foreign element who go to the west and vote there. The government is not concerned over our citizenship ; it may be good, bad or indifferent. What the government is interested in is how many votes they will get out of this particular bill. We have a great many foreigners in the city from which I come, and the number is continually growing through new arrivals. The two great railways are bringing foreigners into Toronto under no known law of immigration and under the new antiimmigration law. There are a large number of applications for naturalization in the county of York every time the court of sessions meets. They have five or six county court judges, and the applicants appear before them, witnesses can be heard, and the applicants examined, if necessary, to find out whether they appreciate our citizenship and would make good citizens, and after the judge has determined upon the fitness of the applicant, a certificate is issued, and naturalization papers are granted by the government. That system has worked well, buit now it is proposed in the twinkling of an eye to change all that, and to centralize all this work in the city of Ottawa in the Secretary of State's office where no doubt the minister will gather around him a large number of government officials appointed by the Liberal party, who will see that these certificates are issued at so much per head. We know that in order to get a job to-day, even though you are a returned soldier, you have to join the Liberal ward association and pay a dollar. Is that going to be the process here, and also to obtain naturalization papers under the proposed act?
I do not wish to criticize a young minister but I fear that his department will become a huge political machine, especially around election time, for coining out these certificates of naturalization irrespective of the fitness of the applicant. The minister last night read the history of naturalization the world over from time immemorial, referring to the French system, the English system, the system in the United States and in Australia. Let me tell him that the position he gave last night as that of the United States is not the position in the United States to-day at all. The United States are tightening up their restrictions all along the line, in immigration, naturalization and colonization. They have their quota
Naturalization Act

system of immigration, and they are tightening up their naturalization system, putting the brakes on and stiffening the regulations all along the line. No matter what country you come from, once you enter the United States, you have to become an American citizen. There is only one flag and only one school there. We have to admire the American people for knowing how to make people become American citizens and respect the law and flag and their institutions. There is no catering there to the foreign way of things.
The minister also referred to Australia. I should like to refer to a speech made by the Prime Minister of Australia, in which he said that Australia is going to be kept a white man's country, that their conditions are different from those in the United States and Canada, and that they are not going to open the flood gates to European immigration. As a result of that policy on the part of Australia, Canada is losing the British immigrant. They are going to Australia and New Zealand, which are doing all the windowdressing in the old country to-day and getting the vast bulk of all immigration from the land.
Naturalization is a very live question, Mr. Chairman, and it is closely allied to the question of immigration, and the question of sedition which we were discussing the other night in this house. I am very sorry that parliament saw fit to remove the provision we had on the statute book with regard to sedition. There is a large body of public opinion in this country that is opposed to any changes being made in that act, and I know that many Liberals as well were opposed to repealing that provision.
This bill we have before us will mean that all the work of naturalization will be centered in the city of Ottawa, and the Secretary of State will have power to decide who shall become naturalized and who shall not. It will simply mean the building up of a huge political machine for the issuing of certificates of naturalization, just as the customs service was a political machine in the old days. Agents of the government in all the large centres from Vancouver to the Atlantic seaboard will be issuing certificates of naturalization in a haphazard way just before election time, with no regard for maintaining our citizenship at its present standard, and we will have instead of county court administration as now, a political administration. I should like to refer to an article that was written to the Toronto Globe yesterday by a great bishop of the Anglican church, who would no doubt be criticized here because he

stands four-square for the British Empire. I refer to Bishop Lloyd, of Saskatoon. He protests against any change being made in this act. Then, in addition, we have the opinion of the county court judges that the present act is working admirably and should not be removed from the statute books, especially at this time owing to the unrest in the country, and with so many foreigners entering Canada. If Canada is going to remain a British country, we want a British immigration policy, and we should not be wiping off the statute book acts that are for the preservation and protection of our citizenship. If Canada is not going to continue to be a British country, let us know. I wish to protest against the repeal of the provision regarding sedition, and protest also against repealing these sections of the Naturalization Act which have worked out admirably.
Furthermore, it will cost hundreds and thousands of dollars to enforce this act, and in the end it will be a mere farce, because certificates will be handed out just as they used to hand out script years ago, and the result will be that the quality of our citizenship will be lowered. Coming from a city in which there is a large number of foreigners, applying for naturalization at the general sessions for York where the Naturalization Act is working out very well, according to the opinion of the county court judges, I protest against the changes that are being made in this bill.

This measure is so important and so far-reaching in its effects, not only upon the present population of Canada, but upon the many thousands who are coming and will come into this country, that it warrants the dose scrutiny and study of every member of this house. Not only that, the measure is of such a nature that I think it warrants the condemnation of every member of this house. I have a very considerable respect and regard for the ability and sincerity of the hon. minister who introduced this measure, but in considering a measure of this kind we must have regard to its effect upon the community as a whole. After all, the real point of contention in the bill is the elimination of the courts from deciding upon the qualifications of an applicant for citizenship, and replacing that authority with agents appointed by the Secretary of State, who will be empowered to determine the qualifications of the applicants for citizenship. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is the pith of this measure.
What are the reasons for this proposed change? Where is the public demand for such

Procedure in Divorce Bills
a fundamental departure from our course of procedure in relation to naturalization? Throughout his whole speech the Secretary of State has not indicated that there is any such demand. His chief arguments are centred around the inconvenience to which some applicants for naturalization are subjected. The minister informs us that representations have been made to him in this respect. I have read his speech carefully and annotated his arguments and reasons for this proposed change. They are six in number. First, the distance from the court of the applicant, and his expense in getting there. That condition prevails only in a very small portion of the Dominion, relatively speaking. I venture to say that if the figures were available it would be found that fully 95 per cent of those applying for citizenship are not handicapped by that difficulty. Second, the sudden adjournment of the court and the necessity of the applicant's returning in order to renew his application. I submit in all fairness that this is an exceptional case. It is not usual for our courts to adjourn suddenly when there is still business to be attended to. Third, the courts sit too infrequently, and attendance has to be made at inopportune times, when the applicants are harvesting or trapping. Again I say those occasions are very limited. The great majority of our courts sit at regular intervals, applicants are given ample notice in advance, and can arrange their affairs so as to be present. Fourth, the lack of uniformity of procedure and unanimity of judgment in determining the qualifications of applicants. With respect to this point, Mr. Chairman, I do not think I can complete my remarks between now and six o'clock.
At six o'clock the Deputy Speaker resumed the chair, and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext: Mr. Anderson moves that Bill No. 150, for the relief of Olive Druker, be now read the third time.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
In accordance with a notice of motion given the other day I move the following amendment:
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it as follows:-
1.	That section one of the bill be amended by adding the following words thereto:-
"and the said Olive Hawkes shall have the custody of their child, and the said Maurice Druker shall pay annually to Olive Hawkes, for her support and maintenance, the sum of five hundred dollars, so long as she remains unmarried; and the sum of two hundred dollars annually for the support and education of their child."
2.	That the following section be added to the said bill:-
"3. The said Maurice Druker shall not have the right to marry again, and if he goes

Procedure in Divorce Bills

through any form of marriage, he shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to seven years' imprisonment, and such marriage shall be null and void."
The other evening I stated my purpose in selecting several of these bills for discussion. In this particular case I am quite willing that the applicant should be granted the divorce, but my purpose is to impress upon the house the necessity of establishing a divorce court in which such matters can be properly attended to. I think it is abundantly evident, from the proceedings of the last few private members' days, that we are not treating these divorce cases in the manner in which they ought to be treated. In order to indicate some of the principles which it would seem to me should be considered in a case of this kind, I chose two test cases. One, introduced the other evening, was a case in which there was involved the custody of the child as well as alimony to the woman; and also in which both individuals were diseased, and I urged that they should not be given the right to marry again so long as this diseased condition continued.
We have in this particular bill still another condition by reason of which I urge that the man should not be granted the right to remarry. I may say that since bringing up this matter in the house I have received a considerable number of communications on the subject. I should like to read a paragraph or so to indicate the state of public opinion in this regard. I quote first from a letter received from a lawyer in western Ontario :
The House of Commons seems to have got the idea that the Ontario divorce court bill sponsored by Mr. A. N. Smith in the commons, is merely a bill for the relief of the senate. In fact it is for the relief of hundreds of people who are too poor to ever get their troubles to the senate. There is a most pitiful cry of the poor of this province for this relief, a low almost inarticulate cry, as is usual -with the cry of the poor, for that chance of le-establisliing homes which the people of the western provinces have.
1 have another letter from a poor woman in Detroit who had read in the newspapers concerning the action taken in this house. From this letter I will extract one paragraph.
I see that you are asking that a man should be made to support his wife and children, also that he be a fit man to marry again. I am a Toronto girl, born and raised there; if there had been such a law I would not be the unhappy woman I am to-day.
Cases of this kind could be multiplied, and I know that every one of these cases means a tragedy in the home life of some couple.
It has been said that an amendment such as I am introducing might be considered

ultra vires, but I would point out that the British North America Act very clearly gives to the Dominion parliament control over marriage and divorce, and I take it that that would apply to everything pertaining to marriage and divorce. Further when divorces were first granted in Canada provision was made for the custody of the children and for the payment of alimony, and as far as I have been able to learn the constitutionality of such action never has been challenged. The other evening I read from the Campbell case of 1879, and to-night I venture to repeat one of the paragraphs from the argument by Senator Miller:
Under the British North America Act the legislation in regard to civil rights is given exclusively to the local legislatures, but it cannot be controverted, I think, that when the parliament of Canada has exclusive power to deal with any subject of legislation, that so far as it is necessary to deal with civil rights in connection with such legislation, we have the undoubted power to deal with them, where this parliament has the right to legislate on any subject it must be considered that we have the power to legislate regarding all matters incident to that subject.
I do not wish to develop the legal argument any further; I do not think it necessary. Again, however, it has been claimed by some that the action contemplated in my amendment would be outside the terms of the petition, and that therefore it should not be accepted by this house. I would point out that the last paragraph of the petition carries a standard clause, as follows:
Wherefore your petitioner humbly prays that your honourable house may be pleased to pass an act dissolving the said marriage between your petitioner and the said Maurice Druker and enabling your petitioner to marry again, and granting your petitioner such further and other relief in the premises as to your honourable house may seem meet.
So if we chose to provide for the custody of the child or if we chose to order the payment of alimony' undoubtedly these matters come within the terms of the petition. Aside from that, however, I urge that we have the right to grant divorce on whatever terms are considered advisable by this parliament. There is no limitation to our powers in that regard. It would require a very strong argument indeed to prove that we have no such right.
With regard to this particular case I would point out that the courts of Ontario have already granted the custody of the child as well as alimony, so it might be claimed it is not necessary that we should take action in this regard. However, this case suits me all the better because the courts of Ontario have taken action along these lines, as after all I am introducing this amendment to determine the principle at stake. As I said the

Procedure in Divorce Bills
other evening, if this amendment had been drawn with legal care perhaps we should have inserted a provision as to how the money should be paid; perhaps we should have included penalties for the non-payment of the money. Undoubtedly we should have been able to go more fully into the question as to whether or not these sums suggested are sufficient to provide for the maintenance of the wife and child. I said the other evening that the figures which I suggested were quite arbitrary, because it is quite obvious that we have not before us in this committee or in the house sufficient evidence concerning all the circumstances of the case to know how much should be set aside for the maintenance of the wife and child. Again that is simply an illustration of the necessity for this sort of thing being attended to by a court, where full investigation could be made with regard to all these matters.
There is a second part to my amendment. Ism trying to make provision for the wife and child, and I am also suggesting that the man be not given the right to marry again. I know that the bill before us explicitly gives the woman the right to marry again, and as I said earlier I am quite willing that this should be done. It does seem to me, however, that with this evidence before us we must hesitate to inferentially give this man the right to marry again. In the preamble of this bill as passed by the senate I read the following:
Whereas Olive Druker, residing at the city of London, England, wife of Maurice Druker, manager, who is domiciled in Canada and formerly resided at the city of London, in the province of Ontario, has by her petition alleged that they were married on the sixteenth day of September, A.D. 1924. at the city of London, England, she then being Olive Hawkes, a spinster; and whereas by her petition she has prayed that, because of sodomy committed by him since then, their marriage be dissolved; and whereas the said marriage and the said sodomy have been proved by evidence adduced and it is expedient that the prayer of her petition be granted: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
We have that preamble before us as the basis on which we are granting this woman a divorce, and I submit that we should hesitate to grant the privilege of remarriage to a man who has so cruelly mistreated his wife and who has committed a crime for which he is liable to life imprisonment. Are we going to tell this man he can go scot free and leave him in a position to abuse another wife? I would hope that the time might come when, in cases of sexual perversion of this kind, there might be some sort of surgical operation, which will 56103-163J
provide for such cases better than we are able to do under our present legislation, but until such time arrives I submit that we are hardly justified in turning such a man loose. So without arguing the case at greater length, I would urge, that in this bill we incorporate each of the provisions, to which I have referred, namely, that the wife be given custody of the child, that alimony be provided for her and maintenance for her child, and that the man be refused the right to marry again.

Although this bill is in my name, I am only sponsoring it for the solicitor in charge for the petitioner, but as the matter is entrusted to me I think it is only fair that something should be said on her behalf here. One has only to read the petition and, if one is so disposed, the evidence which has been sent to us from the senate, to see the nature of the offence and I feel justified in thinking that the senate committee has reported properly. The offence is a crime which, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, is punishable by life imprisonment, and accompanying that crime were other offences against the criminal code, also adultery practices.
This petition is offered on behalf of the wife, who desires to have the marriage bond dissolved because of those crimes and offences against the marital bond. The amendments, it seems to me, are intended to make the granting of that divorce conditional. We must not forget that the remedy here is asked for by the wife, the injured person, not by the one who committed the wrong. Whether parliament would be justified in carrying a penalty to the one who does the wrong is another matter, and it appears to me that the amendment is one that should be dealt with by parliament in a separate bill that might be made applicable to every divorce application which comes before parliament. All that the petitioner asks for is the dissolution of the marriage tie. The senate committee, I submit, found in favour of her application, and they recommend that the bill be passed. The evidence shows that the petitioner and her witnesses proved, not only the crimes alleged but also that the respondent had deprived her of moneys that she had of her own before marriage, and that she holds a judgment against her husband for the amount involved in that respect. The evidence further shows that she proceeded in the courts of Ontario and obtained a judgment for alimony, not of $500, as this amendment would say, but of $250 a month or $3,000 a year. Furthermore, the evidence also establishes that at the time
Procedure in Divorce Bills

that judgment was signed, in October last, she was entitled to SI ,500 by way of arrears of alimony, and that judgment has not been purged by payment. Further than that, I have before me a copy of an order made in the supreme court of Ontario on the 22nd of December last, by which she is awarded the custody of the child, which is under three years of age. I might say also that the husband bad converted some of his wife's goods and chattels, to the amount of some $7,000, and she has a judgment for that in the courts of Ontario. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but she has proceeded in the courts of Michigan and she has there obtained judgment for the value of the goods that he converted, and she also has proceeded to obtain a confirmation in the American courts of the judgment that she holds in Ontario for alimony, and also for the custody of the child.	_
I think it should be pointed out here, in view of what has been said by the hon. member, that the application did not go by default; the respondent appeared before the senate committee and gave sworn evidence, yet he did not in one word attempt to deny the bestiality of the crimes which she _ had testified to; all he did was oppose the petition on the ground that he was an American citizen, or that he was domiciled in the United States. It was also brought out that he has not become an American citizen but that he has filed papers looking to the acquirement of citizenship in the United States.
It may be noted that the first part of the amendment which was moved by the member for Winnipeg North Centre has already been satisfied by the courts of Ontario and Michigan. That is, the petitioner has already got what this amendment would like to give her in that respect. As to the moneys due her from her husband, she has failed to realize on the judgment obtained; they are of no use, because the officers of the court have not been able to implement them. The fact that he has applied for citizenship in the United States indicates that he does not intend to make this country his domicile, and the last part of the amendment would apply only if he remained in Canada. Our law is not enforceable in the United States; it is enforceable only in Canada. If he married again he would be responsible, probably, to the extent of the penalty prescribed by the amendment, but it is quite evident that he intends to live in the United States, not in Canada. He is permanently employed in the country to the south, being in business in the city of Detroit. So that the adoption of this proposed amendment would really be an in-
effective measure; I do not think the bill dissolving the marriage should be burdened by this amendment, because of its ineffectiveness in Canada owing to his being in another country.
I feel very much the same as the member for Winnipeg North Centre, that these cases should be tried in the courts of Ontario, but that is a matter dealt with by another bill. If such a law were in force to-day I have no doubt that the courts of Ontario would give the wife in this case all the remedies that she desires. The courts of Ontario, as those of other provinces, have power to grant alimony and determine the, custody of the children, and that sort of thing. Why is it necessary for us to legislate further in that regard?
On the question of the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, I am not going to offer any extended remarks. The British North America Act says that the federal parliament can legislate with regard to marriage and divorce, and the provinces in respect to the solemnization of marriage. It might be argued that if this amendment passed we should be declaring that the respondent is ineligible for marriage, and as something which precedes another marriage it might be determined possibly under the question of solemnization. The Ontario law already provides for something of the same kind in the case of infants; it prescribes that infants may not marry without the consent of their parents, and so on. If the province has power to prescribe even to the extent of who shall marry, it could easily be argued that if we in our legislation prohibit this man from marrying again, we are attempting to do something that is within the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario.
I submit that the amendment should be voted down and that the bill should be allowed to pass as it stands. What is included in the amendment should be brought before the house in a separate bill so that it may be applicable to all divorces granted by parliament. It is for parliament to decide whether or not conditions of that character should be before the courts in determining the question of divorce, but in this case there is no reason at all for such an amendment. This woman is without doubt entitled to a divorce; the amendment only complicates the matter, and I doubt very much whether we have power to punish the man and whether, if we endeavoured to do so, such punishment would be effective.

Procedure in Divorce Bills

This subject has been brought before the house a number of times by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). As it has not been my privilege to be present at any time during the discussion, perhaps I might be permitted to say a word or two on the matter. The duty has been delegated to me of representing the private bills committee on the senate committee on divorce. It is not altogether a pleasant duty and I am not going to say that I have adequately discharged it, but on various occasions I have attended meetings of the senate committee and I have watched the proceedings. If I read Hansard aright, when this matter was under discussion before, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) referred to the way in which cases were submitted before that committee and I wish very heartily to endorse the testimony which they gave at that time. It is a great mistake that the opinion should be allowed to go out to the country that these matters are not considered seriously by parliament. The faot that these discussions have taken place in the house will tend to increase throughout Canada the opinion that we are dealing with these matters in a careless, haphazard fashion. That is not the case. As I have said, in the discharge of the duty imposed upon me by the private bills committee, I have on various occasions attended meetings of the senate committee. I have been greatly impressed by the care that has been exercised by the senators in coming to conclusions and regarding the character of the evidence which they are prepared to accept. As we know, there is only one ground on which divorce is granted by that committee and a petition is granted not simply because that offence is suspected but because it is proven by incontrovertible evidence. Therefore when these bills come before the house, supposing that they may go through in a somewhat formal manner, perhaps those not acquainted with the previous procedure may think proper consideration has not been given to them. That is not the case. Those cases are well considered; in the great majority of them no defence is offered and the respondent does not appear because the case is too conclusive against him and judgment, I find, is invariably rendered in accordance with the evidence. If we are to consider the bills in this house in the same manner and with the same degree of care that they are considered in the senate, it will be necessary for us to have all the evidence adduced before the private bills committee and again brought up in the house, and I ask hon. gentlemen: Is it desirable that that should be done? I say most emphatically that it is not desirable.
May I remind the house that the senate is asking to be relieved of the duty and responsibility of passing upon these bills and, indeed, of handling the question of divorce at all?

question.

On section 1-Extension of time for commencement and completion.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAT RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I understand that this
railway goes into the Rouyn district, where there are already two railways. I would ask the Minister of Railways, if he is supporting this bill, to give us his reasons why a third railway should be allowed to go into that district and compete with the other two. Is there not going to be a duplication of railways in that district if this bill goes through?

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAT RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: This is a private bill. Before the railway committee, when this and one other railway bill were under consideration, I pointed out as nearly as I could the situation which would exist in the district in question. The representatives of the railway companies interested also addressed the committee, and all expressed themselves as quite satisfied with what was being done with respect to both of the charters under consideration. Apparently the committee was satisfied that there was plenty of room in that district for the railways in question, and they agreed to report the bill without amendment.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAT RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I cannot but think that we should be very careful about a matter of this kind. This is territory in which we are spending large sums of money. We own the terminals at Hudson bay, and we own at present the only line of railway that reaches the Hudson bay. The minister pointed out
[Mr. Lapointe.l
the other day, very properly, in connection with a railway in northern Alberta, if my memory serves me, that the territory was being invaded by a private line which, if successful, would be able to take away traffic from the government road. Should we not decline absolutely to grant charters to private enterprises where the effect will be in any way to lessen and impair the possibility of our own line earning money, and should we not rather extend branch lines into that territory for the purpose of preserving it for our own railway? In other words, if we must pay the deficits, and we must, let us be very astute to see that so far as possible every bit of territory that is contiguous to our line may be served by profitable branch lines for the protection of our own property.

maintopic: INTERPROVINCIAL AND JAMES BAT RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: If I remember rightly, it was pointed out in the committee that this line parallels the line under another charter which has already been granted, and the question was if they would not both be going through the same territory if both went round the one side of a certain lake. I think we should be careful in granting these charters, particularly to companies of this kind, which is not either of the two great national companies, the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific. It seems to me that we are fast creating another railway situation which in a few years is going to land us in a worse position than the one from which we have been trying to extricate ourselves in the last nine or ten years. We are paralleling lin-es all over this country, and here in this new district we are granting a charter to a new railway company altogether which is going to parallel the line and interfere with the earnings of the Canadian National Railway. We are doing this in many places throughout the Dominion to-day, and I think this parliament should be very careful to see that we do not create a situation which gives rise to a worse railway problem than the one we are now trying to find a solution for. This railway is certainly endeavouring to be first to get into this mining district. Whether it is for the purpose of developing a certain company's mine or not, I do not know, but this makes the third railway in that district, and I repeat, it is invading Canadian National territory and going to interfere with the earnings of our national railway.

I see no reason why parliament should give an extension every five years to this railway. They have already had five extensions from this parliament. Who are these people? The bill doesn't say who they are. This is a very important territory surrounding the towns of Latchford and New Liskeard, and the railway is to run through the townships of Coleman, Bucke, Dymond, Harris and Casey to a point on or near Blanche river, thence in a northerly direction to a point at or near Windigo lake, thence northeasterly to a point on the line of the National Transcontinental at or near the Matagami river. They received their charter in 1907, by chapter 112, and it was renewed in 1908 by chapter 135; they came back five years later, in 1913, for a further extension, by chapter 160; they were back again in another five years, in 1918, for a further extension, by chapter 56, and back again in 1923, for a further extension, by chapter 80, and now in 1928. another five years, they are
back again for another extension. Five years seems to be the psychological moment for them to come back and ask for an extension, with every new parliament. Where is all this going to end? Some of the most important mining districts in Canada to-day are in the territory which this railway is to run through, and I maintain that the territory, no matter who owns this railway, should be served by the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, which is not asking for any subsidy or extension from this legislature.

If my hon. friend will
permit me, the Nipissing Central railway is owned by the Ontario government, and it is the Ontario government which is asking for this extension of time.

The house in committee on Bill No. 71, to incorporate the St. Lawrence River Bridge Company-Mr. Smith (Stormont)-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

This bill should not be allowed to pass in its present form, Mr. Chairman, in view of the action taken by Governor Smith of the state of New York. He has laid down the principle that such international bridges should be built by the state or federal government or by the municipal authority. This parliament has jurisdiction over bridges that are international, interprovincial or that affect navigation.
What is the policy of the government of Canada in regard to this and the other bridge bills? We have three of these bridge bills, one at Sarnia, two or three at Niagara, and two on the St. Lawrence. We are told that the St. Lawrence river question cannot be discussed at the present time because it is on the way to the privy council, but navigation is also affected by this particular private bill. So the issues involved in the reference to the supreme court are relevant to this bill. The interests of navigation are paramount to
Private Bills

any private bill or interests. I protest against this policy. The preamble recites:
Whereas a petition has been presented praying that the persons hereinafter mentioned may be incorporated for the purpose of constructing and operating a bridge for railway and general traffic purposes across the St. Lawrence river from the town of Broekville in the province of Ontario, to a point at or near Morristown, in the state of New York-
Section 1 discloses the personnel of those who have been incorporated to build the proposed bridge. They are:
The Right Honourable George Perry Graham, senator, and James Gill Gardner, manufacturer, both of the town of Broekville, in the province of Ontario.
The latter gentleman is one of the directors of the national railways. In fact, several gentlemen connected with the national railways are behind these bridge bills. The other day an engineer of this railway was a promoter of the Sarnia bridge bill. I contend that if anybody should build bridges it is the Canadian National Railways, but the management say they have nothing to do with such projects. It is well known that a large part of the earnings of the road is being diverted by motor busses and motor trucks engaged in local business. This business should be developed near these bridges by the railway management as a feeder to the main line. Another of the incorporators is William Arthur McLean, of the city of Toronto, consulting engineer. For a number of years he was with the highways branch of the Public Works department of Ontario. We seem to be continually playing the game of bridge both inside and ouside of this building; everybody is playing bridge, it seems, this session. When we ask in the railway committee what is the policy of the government in regard to any private bill for a railway or a bridge, and the Minister of Railways is not present, we are told they have no particular policy. Wherever there is a potential gold mine in the way of traffic the national railways have no money to spend; but wherever there is going to be a deficit, such as the branch line business or a hotel venture in Halifax, or an hotel in Paris, they are ready to spend money like water. This bridge should be built by the people and for the people, or by the two governments or the municipal authority. In other words, the national railways should preserve the territory to be served by this bridge as a feeder for their main line. What did Hon. Alfred Smith, governor of New York, say as to his policy with resDe't to this bridge? I quote:
"Such bridges should be built by the state or states or by one or more governmental subdivisions or by a public municipal authority

similar to the port authority," the governor declared in his blanket veto of the three measures. "If such a bridge is to be built over international waters it should be constructed jointly by the United States in conjunction with the Canadian government or by the state of New York in conjunction with the Canadian province affected."
Such projects, the governor felt could be financed at lower cost by the state or federal governments, while, he added, "they are in their very nature public; to authorize privately-owned toll bridges is a step as backward as to authorize privately-owned highways, under the wording of these acts, the franchise is practically made perpetual."
"If it pays private corporations to erect these bridges," the governor's memorandum continued, "it will certainly pay the state to do it. If tolls are to be charged, the state should be the recipient of the tolls, and they should not be in excess of what is required to operate and maintain property, pay the interest on the bonds and make the necessary annual contributions to the sinking fund for their retirement."
These are Hon. Mr. Smith's views for the state of New York-public ownership for this bridge between the two countries.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, to amend the Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinfret

Mr. Johnston in the chair.

When the committee rose
at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I had not finished my remarks, but the Secretary of State has a statement to make, and I will proceed after he has concluded.

I do not rise to discuss
at any length the remarks made by other hon. gentlemen. I stated the case rather fully last night on the second reading of the bill and many of the remarks that have since followed have answered one another. I believe that opportunity should be given every hon. member interested in the bill to present his views as best he sees fit. I do desire, however, to move an amendment to the section now under consideration and that is my purpose in rising at the moment.
Last night, on the second reading of the bill, I endeavoured to indicate the principle underlying the bill, which is to repeal those clauses whereby an applicant is required to go before the courts, and instead to give to

Naturalization Act
the Secretary of State full discretion to consider, either favourably or unfavourably, any application for naturalization. This, I pointed out, is the principle which obtains in Great Britain and in other British dominions as well. The discussion that has taken place since has not disproved that position, but it has been shown by other hon. gentlemen that there might be this difference between the bill as now proposed and the acts in the different dominions:	that whilst in this
country, if the bill remained in its present form, regulations would issue from the department, in other dominions some of the regulations are made statutory. I appreciate that difference and that is why I am now bringing in this amendment.
I had intended in committee explaining the procedure that would be followed by the department, should this bill be adopted^ The applicant would have to send his application to the Secretary of State on a prescribed form, as is done now; and that form is quite expansive, covering all the requirements of the act and also affording an opportunity for ample information on every point involved. The form is sworn by the applicant before a justice of the peace, a commissioner of the superior court, or other person competent for the purpose, and it is intended not only to retain that regulation but, if necessary, to add to the references that will be required to accompany it. It was also the intention of the department, through regulations, to have the fullest investigation conducted into all the facts of every individual case and to give, as is done in other dominions, some degree of publicity to the request for a certificate.
I intimated to the hon. member for Fort William that in the present bill it would be possible in certain cases for the Secretary of State to grant a certificate immediately, without any delay at all. I will say frankly that such was the intention, for this reason: In certain cases where the applicants were well known to the department, and when it was quite easy to verify their application, it would have been desirable that the certificate be granted at once. And I had in mind only exceptional cases of that character. But it was clearly my intention, through regulations, to institute the most severe investigation in every case. But it is impossible to conduct any such investigation except in a period of at least thirty or forty days. I will admit also that from the discussion which has taken place in the house, and from the view
generally expressed on all sides, the discretion of the Secretary of State, possibly, should not be made too wide. I have been convinced that it might be better to lose sight of these exceptional cases and to provide for a compulsory delay, and that is the object of the amendment which I now wish to propose. In this amendment it will be stipulated that the applicant shall apply to the Secretary of State on a prescribed form; that the application shall be posted in the post office nearest to the residence of the applicant: and that a compulsory delay of not less than sixty days shall take place before the certificate is granted. All these stipulations were contemplated in the regulations which the department, through myself, would have submitted in the committee stage. I am, however, quite willing to make them statutory, in my great desire if possible to bring about an understanding in regard to this bill. I believe that the amendment which I shall submit to the committee will be acceptable, and that the trend of opposition which has been advanced against the bill will in very large measure disappear. I therefore move:
That the following be inserted after the word '"repealed", and the following section be substituted therefor:
22. An alien desiring to be naturalized shall make application therefor in the prescribed form arid forward his application to the minister. The minister shall then send notice of such application to the postmaster at the post office nearest to the place of residence of the applicant, and such postmaster shall thereupon post such notice in a prominent place in the said post office and advise the minister thereof. Such posting shall be made at least sixty days before the issue of the certificate of naturalization.
What does the hon. gentleman expect to gain by this procedure?

The proposed amendment is undoubtedly a step in the right direction, but it does not go very far; the minister ought to take a leap. He remarks that the trend of the opposition will likely disappear in view of this amendment. Well, in my judgment, after listening to the remarks that have been made, the minister has not touched the real point of objection on the part of a large number of those who oppose the bill. The real point of the objection-in fact, the essential feature of the entire bill-is the step now proposed of taking from the courts the decision as to the fitness and the qualifications of the applicant for citizenship and giving that authority exclusively to the Secretary of State-and I am not at all referring to the minister personally. That in my judgment

In 1871 of our then population 60.5 per cent were British, and by 1921 that percentage had fallen to 55.3, the French portion of the population of Canada amounted to 31.2 per cent in 1871, and that figure was reduced by 1921 to 28 per cent. If there are inconveniences in connection with voting, they can easily be remedied by the applicant who desires to vote coming within the law. We are endeavouring to assert what Sir Wilfrid Laurier asserted, that the basis of naturalization in Canada has been a judicial inquiry. That is what he said in his speech on the Naturalization Act. I have not the time to determine when the first naturalization statute was passed, but I do say this, that until the introduction of this bill the Liberal party had expressed itself in the house as being in favour of a judicial investigation in regard to naturalization. Is it possible that all these sixty years of history in connection with the matter should be undone? It is not a question of Conservatism or Toryism. It is purely a question that affects this whole country regardless of party, and when the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) desires to compare the position of the Uitlanders in the Transvaal some years ago with the position that prevails in Canada to-day, I find it a little difficult to follow him

a difficulty that I should think must be felt by most hon. members. We have a Franchise Act that confers the right to vote on all British subjects under certain conditions of residence. Whether a man becomes a British subject or not he himself must determine; and if in the province of Saskatchewan there are difficulties about the courts, I desire to tell him that there is not a single constituency in Alberta, whether on the frontier or otherwise, where there are not district courts to which all persons may resort with respect to claims up to $600, and the judges in those courts have jurisdiction with respect to naturalization.
